network.overall_strategy: This is a connected, conditional synthesis network, not a claim that ten complete prebiotic syntheses of free cysteine have been demonstrated. It contains ten distinct reaction sequences: nine combinations of three activation branches and three sulfur-installation branches, plus an empirical atmospheric-haze route. The protected-cysteine branches follow Foden et al. (2020), but their proposed hydrolysis and deacetylation steps to free cysteine remain unresolved experimental gaps. The phosphate branch additionally requires an unverified precursor-forming step. Glycolaldehyde and HCN provide simple carbon feedstocks; N-acetylimidazole, diamidophosphate and ferricyanide are conditional reagent inputs whose geochemical supply is not established here. All reactions occur in surface settings because the supplied evidence does not establish hydrothermal cysteine synthesis, and hot conditions threaten thiol survival. Photochemistry, oxidative activation, sulfide addition and product preservation require separate stages; this is not a demonstrated one-pot system. No molecular oxygen or enzymes are used. Late-stage products require anoxic, UV-shielded handling and separation from residual oxidants and nitriles. Stereochemistry is unspecified, with racemic products expected absent an asymmetric influence. Neutral parent formulas generally represent acid-base pools. Coproducts use the role intermediate because the schema has no coproduct category. Sulfur and water outputs in the explicitly labeled lumped reactions provide formal elemental bookkeeping, not experimentally established exclusive product distributions.

molecules.common_name: Diamidophosphate, represented as its neutral parent acid
Orthophosphate, represented as its neutral parent acid

reactions.name: Strecker formation of serine nitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic, concentrated aqueous glycolaldehyde and ammonium cyanide; near-neutral to mildly alkaline speciation. Retain volatile HCN and ammonia. Subsequent chemistry requires staged reagent delivery.

reactions.mechanism: Glycolaldehyde and ammonia form an imine or iminium intermediate; cyanide addition gives the alpha-aminonitrile. Water is the net condensation coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) describe serine nitrile as the stable Strecker product of glycolaldehyde, formed in greater than 90% yield with ammonium cyanide. Patel et al. (2015) support a photochemical source of glycolaldehyde but do not establish a continuously operating, geochemically closed system. Glycolaldehyde is therefore an explicit simple feedstock here rather than an invented upstream reaction.

reactions.name: Oxidative N,O-diacetylation with thioacetic acid
agents: Ferricyanide: consumed oxidant, explicitly represented as an input; not a catalyst

conditions.other: Near-neutral buffered water; approximately 1 h in the reported optimized experiment. Requires sufficient acyl donor and oxidant for both N- and O-acetylation. Residual ferricyanide must be exhausted or separated before subsequent sulfide and thiol chemistry.

reactions.mechanism: Oxidative activation of thioacetate enables acyl transfer to the amino and hydroxyl groups. Ferricyanide is reduced to ferrocyanide. The listed elemental sulfur is a formal oxidized-sulfur endpoint for the lumped net reaction, not an assigned elementary intermediate or exclusive measured coproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report up to 91% N,O-diacetylserine nitrile from thioacetic acid and ferricyanide. The transformation is experimentally supported, but concentrated ferricyanide in an otherwise reducing, sulfidic landscape is a substantial geochemical constraint. The formal sulfur balance does not establish actual polysulfide distributions or experimental oxidant consumption. This route uses no molecular oxygen.

reactions.name: N,O-diacetylation with N-acetylimidazole

conditions.other: Near-neutral water with sufficient N-acetylimidazole for both acetyl transfers. Competition from acyl-donor hydrolysis requires concentrated reactants and staged addition.

reactions.mechanism: Nucleophilic acyl substitution transfers acetyl groups to the amine and alcohol, releasing imidazole. N-acetylimidazole is a consumed reagent rather than a catalyst.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report N-acetylimidazole as an effective alternative to thioacetic acid and ferricyanide. This branch avoids exposing the substrate to a stoichiometric oxidant, but the supplied research does not establish a geochemical source or sustained concentration of N-acetylimidazole. Its availability is an explicit boundary assumption.

reactions.name: Nitrile-enabled beta-elimination of acetate

conditions.other: pH approximately 8; approximately 4 days. Buffered, anoxic water. Acetic acid represents the predominantly acetate coproduct at this pH.

reactions.mechanism: The alpha-nitrile enables deprotonation and beta-elimination of the O-acetyl group, creating the activated alkene. N-acetylation stabilizes the dehydroalanine-type product against destructive tautomerization.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report approximately 85% conversion after four days at room temperature, with an optimum around pH 8. This is a documented kinetic bottleneck. The nitrile and N-acyl protection are mechanistically important; an unprotected dehydroalanine or an amide analogue cannot simply be substituted with the same expected performance.

reactions.name: Speculative activated phosphorylation of serine nitrile

conditions.other: Proposed mildly acidic to neutral concentrated solution, followed by rehydration. Diamidophosphate is a conditional supplied reagent. No validated time, yield or selective phosphorylation condition is available for this substrate.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed alcohol attack at activated phosphorus, followed by hydrolysis of residual P-N bonds, would produce the phosphate monoester and release ammonia. This node lumps that unverified sequence into an element-balanced net transformation.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE: the supplied research does not demonstrate diamidophosphate phosphorylation of serine nitrile. Foden et al. (2020) support downstream chemistry of O-phosphoserine nitrile, not this route to that precursor. Activated phosphorus chemistry motivates the proposal, but competing N-phosphorylation, nitrile hydrolysis and reagent availability could prevent it. This edge exposes the phosphate branch's precursor gap rather than treating an activated intermediate as a simple feedstock.

reactions.name: N-acetylation of O-phosphoserine nitrile

conditions.other: Near-neutral water; sufficient acyl donor for N-acetylation. The exact reagent-specific protocol for this implementation is not established by the supplied report.

reactions.mechanism: The amino group undergoes nucleophilic acetyl transfer from N-acetylimidazole, releasing imidazole while retaining the phosphate leaving group.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report N-acetyl-O-phosphoserine nitrile formation at approximately 80% yield and separately establish N-acetylimidazole as an effective acyl donor for serine nitrile. SPECULATIVE IMPLEMENTATION: the supplied report does not establish that this exact donor and condition combination gives the reported phosphate-substrate yield. No 80% yield is assigned to this modeled edge.

reactions.name: Magnesium-promoted beta-elimination of phosphate
agents: Dissolved Mg2+: Lewis-acid promoter of phosphate elimination

conditions.other: pH approximately 7; approximately 1 day for the reported magnesium-promoted experiment. Cool the solution before thiol installation. Avoid assuming that every phosphate-bearing mineral supplies adequate dissolved Mg2+.

reactions.mechanism: Beta-elimination releases inorganic phosphate and forms the same N-acetylated dehydroalanine nitrile reached through acetate elimination. Mg2+ promotes the phosphate-leaving-group pathway.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report approximately 24% product after one day with Mg2+, compared with approximately 8% after three days without that promotion at 60 degrees Celsius and pH 7. This branch is experimentally motivated but less productive than the acetate branch. Its heating occurs before the fragile cysteinyl thiol is installed.

reactions.name: Direct sulfide addition and nitrile thioamidation

conditions.temperature: 300-333 K; use the cool end for product preservation
conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 atm with restricted gas exchange
conditions.other: Near-neutral sulfidic water; sufficient sulfide for both alkene addition and nitrile conversion. UV-shielded, anoxic conditions with no residual ferricyanide.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide adds across the activated carbon-carbon double bond to install the beta-thiol. Additional sulfide converts the nitrile functionality into a thioamide. This is a lumped tandem transformation, not merely alkene addition.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report near-quantitative formation of N-acetylcysteine thioamide from N-acetyldehydroalanine nitrile and H2S. The product is neither free cysteine nor simply its unmodified nitrile. N-protection is retained because unprotected aminothiol/aminonitrile chemistry favors destructive cyclization and condensation.

reactions.name: Thioacetate conjugate addition to the activated alkene

conditions.other: pH approximately 7; approximately 12 h. Anoxic, UV-shielded water. No oxidative activation is needed for this sulfur-addition step.

reactions.mechanism: Thioacetate performs conjugate addition to the activated alkene, yielding an S-acetyl-protected cysteine nitrile while preserving the N-acetyl group.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report quantitative thioester formation within approximately 12 h at pH 7. This is a supported alternative to direct H2S treatment and creates a genuine branch point between ammonolytic and sulfidolytic sulfur deprotection.

reactions.name: Ammonolytic removal of the S-acetyl group

conditions.temperature: 300-333 K, modeled window; exact optimum not supplied
conditions.other: Ammonia-containing water; proposed near-neutral to mildly alkaline speciation. Separate this operation from residual oxidants and avoid unnecessary heating. Exact concentration and residence time require the original experimental protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia attacks the S-acetyl thioester, producing acetamide and the free side-chain thiol. The N-acetyl group and nitrile remain intact.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report N-acetylcysteine nitrile in 77% yield through ammonolysis. The cited yield belongs to the reported experiment, not every condition in the modeled window. Selective thioester cleavage is chemically preferable to attempting premature removal of the N-acetyl protection.

reactions.name: Sulfidolytic S-deacetylation coupled to thioamide formation

conditions.temperature: 300-333 K, modeled window; exact optimum not supplied
conditions.other: Near-neutral water with excess sulfide; anoxic and UV-shielded. Requires sufficient sulfide for thioester cleavage and nitrile conversion.

reactions.mechanism: Sulfide cleaves the S-acetyl thioester, formally returning thioacetic acid, and also converts the nitrile to a thioamide. The beta-thiol becomes unmasked while N-acetyl protection is retained.
reactions.reasoning: Foden et al. (2020) report approximately 95% N-acetylcysteine thioamide through the thiolysis branch. This converges with direct H2S treatment but proceeds through a chemically distinct S-acetyl intermediate. The modeled temperature window is not a substitute for the original reagent concentrations and timing.

reactions.name: Speculative hydration of N-acetylcysteine nitrile

conditions.other: Proposed acidic water, approximately pH 1-3; unknown residence time and yield. Anoxic, UV-shielded handling with no free aldehydes or residual oxidants.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-assisted water addition to the nitrile would form an imidic intermediate that tautomerizes to the carboxamide while retaining N-acetyl protection.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE under the stated prebiotic conditions: nitrile hydration is chemically reasonable, but the supplied research does not demonstrate this selective conversion as part of a complete free-cysteine synthesis. Foden et al. (2020) establish the protected nitrile precursor, not a validated downstream release sequence. Intramolecular thiol reactions and slow low-temperature hydrolysis may compete.

reactions.name: Speculative hydrolytic replacement of thioamide sulfur

conditions.other: Proposed acidic water, approximately pH 1-3. Unknown selectivity, rate and required sulfide activity. Preserve anoxia and exclude UV during product handling.

reactions.mechanism: Proposed water addition at the thioamide carbon followed by sulfur elimination would produce the corresponding carboxamide and H2S. Competing hydrolysis channels are not assumed absent.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE: Foden et al. (2020) support formation of N-acetylcysteine thioamide but do not establish this selective low-temperature hydrolysis as a route to free cysteine. Carboxamide formation is a chemically possible channel, not a demonstrated exclusive outcome; thiocarboxylic products, cyclization and decomposition require testing.

reactions.name: Speculative terminal carboxamide hydrolysis

conditions.other: Proposed acidic water, approximately pH 1-2. Unknown residence time; ammonia is predominantly ammonium in situ. No enzyme or selective mineral amidase is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the terminal carboxamide would generate the carboxylic acid and ammonia, with the N-acetyl group ideally retained at this stage.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE as a selective prebiotic step: the supplied research does not establish conversion of these protected amides to N-acetylcysteine under preservation-compatible conditions. Foden et al. (2020) do not close the free-cysteine synthesis. Low-temperature amide hydrolysis may be too slow, while more forcing conditions risk thiol loss and competing cleavage.

reactions.name: Unresolved N-deacetylation to free cysteine

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K, hypothetical test window rather than a validated protocol
conditions.other: Proposed strongly acidic pool, approximately pH 0-2; unknown reaction time, conversion and selectivity. Anoxic and UV-shielded. Exclude residual cyanide, reactive aldehydes and oxidants; avoid hot dry-down.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the N-acetyl amide bond would release free cysteine and acetic acid. The network does not assume that this cleavage is sufficiently rapid or selective to permit cysteine accumulation.
reactions.reasoning: SPECULATIVE AND DECISIVE BOTTLENECK: Foden et al. (2020) do not demonstrate prebiotic deacetylation to free cysteine. This edge expresses the missing chemistry required to reach the requested target, not an established procedure. Rossetto et al. (2022) demonstrate heat-sensitive cysteinyl residues under particular peptide and metal conditions; those data warn against forcing hydrolysis but do not provide a quantitative lifetime for free cysteine in this proposed acidic setting. Every protected-route pathway remains conditional on this step.

reactions.name: Empirical atmospheric-haze source of cysteine

conditions.other: Far-UV irradiation of an anoxic N2-dominated atmosphere containing approximately 0.1% CH4, 0.5% CO2 and 5 ppmv H2S; gas-phase and aerosol chemistry. Accumulation after deposition into water is not established.

reactions.mechanism: Unresolved, many-step photochemical network involving radical production and aerosol chemistry. This node is an empirical source edge, not an elementary reaction. Water permits a formal element-balanced net representation but is not asserted to be the measured or exclusive coproduct; the actual aerosol contains many additional compounds.
reactions.reasoning: Reed et al. (2025) report a cysteine assignment supported by accurate mass, fragmentation, isotopic features and irradiation/sulfide controls. Nevertheless, the evidence comes from one study, provides no isolated cysteine yield, and does not resolve the mechanism or survival after deposition. The proposed ethanethiol-to-cysteamine-to-cysteine sequence is not expanded into invented established reactions. This route provides evidence for free cysteine without the N-deacetylation requirement, but quantitative production and independent replication remain open.

pathways.name: Oxidative acetate activation followed by direct sulfide addition
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde undergoes Strecker conversion, oxidative N,O-acetylation, acetate elimination and direct sulfide treatment. The protected thioamide is experimentally supported; the subsequent hydrolysis and deacetylation sequence to free cysteine is speculative.

pathways.name: Oxidative acetate activation followed by thioacetate addition and ammonolysis
pathways.description: The oxidative acetate branch reaches the activated alkene, which receives thioacetate. Ammonolysis yields the protected cysteine nitrile rather than the thioamide. Nitrile hydration, carboxamide hydrolysis and N-deacetylation remain unvalidated completion steps.

pathways.name: Oxidative acetate activation followed by thioacetate addition and sulfidolysis
pathways.description: An S-acetyl cysteine nitrile intermediate is formed after oxidative precursor activation. Sulfidolysis produces the protected thioamide, distinguishing this sequence from direct H2S addition and ammonolysis. Free-cysteine release remains speculative.

pathways.name: Acetylimidazole activation followed by direct sulfide addition
pathways.description: N-acetylimidazole replaces the oxidative acylation system, avoiding ferricyanide exposure. Direct sulfide treatment forms the protected thioamide. The acetylating reagent's geochemical supply and the final hydrolytic release sequence remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Acetylimidazole activation followed by thioacetate addition and ammonolysis
pathways.description: Nonoxidative acetyl transfer creates the acetate-elimination precursor. Thioacetate addition and ammonolysis then furnish N-acetylcysteine nitrile. This is a distinct reported-chemistry combination, not an independently demonstrated complete synthesis of free cysteine.

pathways.name: Acetylimidazole activation followed by thioacetate addition and sulfidolysis
pathways.description: Acetylimidazole-based activation is combined with the S-acetyl intermediate and sulfidolytic thioamide-forming branch. It avoids a stoichiometric oxidant during activation but retains conditional reagent supply and speculative free-cysteine release.

pathways.name: Phosphate activation followed by direct sulfide addition
pathways.description: A hypothetical phosphorylation supplies the precursor for the experimentally motivated N-acetylated phosphate-elimination branch. Mg2+-promoted elimination precedes direct sulfide addition. Precursor formation, the exact acylation implementation and free-cysteine release remain conditional.

pathways.name: Phosphate activation followed by thioacetate addition and ammonolysis
pathways.description: The conditional phosphate branch is combined with thioacetate addition and ammonolysis to retain a protected cysteine nitrile. Both entry into the phosphate branch and its downstream conversion to free cysteine require unverified chemistry.

pathways.name: Phosphate activation followed by thioacetate addition and sulfidolysis
pathways.description: The conditional phosphate-elimination route reaches the S-acetyl cysteine nitrile and then the protected thioamide through sulfidolysis. Its reaction sequence differs from the other phosphate variants, but it is not a separately validated complete synthesis.

pathways.name: Far-UV atmospheric-haze formation
pathways.description: An empirical, mechanistically unresolved source edge links simple anoxic atmospheric gases to a reported cysteine identification. Unlike P1-P9, it does not require modeled N-deacetylation, but isolated yield, independent replication and post-deposition accumulation remain unestablished.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Foden et al. (2020, Science) strongly support the sequence through N-acetylcysteine thioamide. The supplied evidence does not establish the subsequent thioamide-to-amide conversion, carboxamide hydrolysis or N-deacetylation under cysteine-compatible conditions. Consequently, this is a credible protected-cysteinyl synthesis followed by an unresolved route to free cysteine. Staging addresses oxidant incompatibility conceptually, but oxidant removal and product preservation are not operationally specified.
suggestions: Specify reaction-specific conditions, including approximately pH 8 and the reported multiday room-temperature timescale for rxn_004.
Define and test removal of residual ferricyanide before sulfur installation.
Demonstrate rxn_013–rxn_015 with product identification, conversion measurements and thiol-retention assays; do not infer them from elemental balance.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Thioacetate addition and selective S-deacetylation by ammonolysis align with Foden et al. (2020), including the reported production of N-acetylcysteine nitrile. This establishes neither its selective hydration under the proposed conditions nor the final two hydrolyses. Water appearing as a reactant is insufficient to establish useful hydrolysis rates. Free cysteine remains conditional on resolving these transformations and separating it from residual nitriles.
suggestions: Specify ammonia concentration, pH and residence time for selective S-deacetylation.
Establish a thiol-compatible nitrile-hydration protocol for rxn_012 and measure competing reactions.
Validate carboxamide hydrolysis and N-deacetylation, including product survival after removal of residual oxidants and nitriles.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sulfur-installation sequence agrees with the reported thioacetate-addition and sulfidolysis chemistry of Foden et al. (2020). Its supported endpoint is N-acetylcysteine thioamide, not free cysteine. The alternative sulfur-installation sequence does not resolve the shared downstream hydrolysis and deacetylation bottlenecks. All reactions conserve atoms and charge with the supplied coefficients.
suggestions: Encode the two-H2S stoichiometry of rxn_011 and specify sulfide activity and reaction conditions.
Determine whether rxn_013 selectively produces the stated carboxamide rather than an alternative sulfur-containing product.
Test the complete downstream sequence under anoxic conditions after removing residual oxidant.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: N-acetylimidazole activation, acetate elimination and sulfide addition are supported by the supplied account of Foden et al. (2020). This branch does not require ferricyanide removal, although acetylating-reagent availability and delivery remain conditional. The decisive limitation is unchanged: rxn_013–rxn_015 have not been demonstrated as a compatible sequence releasing free cysteine.
suggestions: Include two equivalents of N-acetylimidazole in the formal stoichiometry and specify conditions controlling competing reagent hydrolysis.
Give quantitative conditions and product distributions for thioamide hydrolysis.
Establish selective N-deacetylation and subsequent free-cysteine survival rather than treating protection removal as automatic.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The route to N-acetylcysteine nitrile is well aligned with Foden et al. (2020). The proposed continuation is chemically conceivable, but no substrate-specific, thiol-compatible hydration and deprotection protocol is supplied. This pathway therefore remains incomplete for the requested free-cysteine target despite strong upstream evidence. Conditional reagent inputs are acceptable assumptions, not demonstrations of environmental availability.
suggestions: Attach experimental citations and numerical conditions to activation, elimination, sulfur addition and ammonolysis.
Measure selective conversion of mol_023 to mol_025 under explicitly defined conditions.
Demonstrate the final hydrolyses and quantify free cysteine with thiol-appropriate analytical methods.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The activation and sulfur-installation chemistry is consistent with the supplied experimental literature. Sulfidolysis produces the protected thioamide and does not itself establish a cysteine carboxyl group or remove N-acetyl protection. The explicit acknowledgment of these gaps is appropriate, but it cannot substitute for evidence that the final sequence operates under the proposed preservation constraints.
suggestions: Specify sulfide concentration, pH and residence time for rxn_011.
Verify the exact product and selectivity of thioamide-to-amide conversion.
Test hydrolysis and deacetylation as an integrated sequence, including sulfur-containing degradation products and free-cysteine recovery.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This branch adds an unverified precursor-forming step: balanced DAP consumption does not demonstrate selective O-phosphorylation of serine nitrile. The subsequent phosphate-elimination chemistry has experimental support, but the supplied literature reports limited conversion at pH 7 and 60 °C, improved by Mg2+. Magnesium availability and reaction conditions are not specified in the network. The same downstream free-cysteine bottlenecks remain.
suggestions: Demonstrate mol_018 formation from DAP and serine nitrile, distinguishing O-phosphorylation from competing products.
Specify Mg2+ availability, concentration and residence time; use the reported low phosphate-elimination conversion when assessing material throughput.
Validate rxn_013–rxn_015 independently rather than assuming that a successful phosphate branch establishes free-cysteine synthesis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Thioacetate addition and ammonolysis are supported, but the pathway depends on both unverified O-phosphoserine-nitrile formation and an unresolved nitrile-hydration/deprotection sequence. Foden et al.'s phosphate-elimination results support rxn_007 conditionally, not high-throughput formation of its precursor from DAP. Its reported conversion and Mg2+ dependence should be retained explicitly. No complete route to free cysteine is demonstrated.
suggestions: Establish selective DAP-mediated formation of the stated phosphate intermediate.
Define the Mg2+-containing elimination stage and transfer to conditions appropriate for sulfur addition and ammonolysis.
Measure nitrile hydration, carboxamide hydrolysis and N-deacetylation, including product recovery across the complete sequence.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The sulfur-installation segment is supported by Foden et al. (2020), but it cannot compensate for the unverified phosphate-precursor synthesis or the unresolved terminal chemistry. Magnesium-promoted phosphate elimination is a demonstrated, condition-dependent transformation with limited reported conversion, not an intrinsically invalid reaction. The overall pathway nevertheless lacks experimental continuity from its starting materials to free cysteine.
suggestions: Identify and quantify the phosphorylation products before assigning mol_018 as an available intermediate.
Add explicit Mg2+ conditions and account for incomplete phosphate elimination.
Demonstrate selective thioamide hydrolysis and subsequent deprotection while monitoring thiol preservation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway provides the strongest evidence for the actual free-cysteine target. Reed et al. (2025, PNAS, doi:10.1073/pnas.2516779122) reported high-resolution mass-spectral, fragmentation, isotopic and control evidence for cysteine in photochemical haze. However, quantitative yield, independent replication, mechanism and survival after deposition remain unresolved. The balanced equation is acceptable as explicitly labeled bookkeeping, not as a measured exclusive conversion or elementary reaction.
suggestions: Specify the atmospheric gas/aerosol compartment, far-UV spectrum and flux, ambient temperature and pressure, and reported feed composition.
Obtain quantitative, thiol-appropriate measurements and independent replication, with orthogonal analytical confirmation where possible.
Model deposition and recovery into anoxic, UV-shielded waters and measure cysteine survival; retain rxn_016 as an empirical source rather than a resolved mechanism.

evaluation.network_feedback: The network is structurally valid and appropriately presented as conditional, but it is not approved at the required overall confidence of 0.9. All 30 molecule nodes and 16 reaction nodes belong to one connected graph, and molecule IDs are used consistently. The deterministic check establishes 10 reactions balanced as written and six balanceable with coefficients; there are no conservation violations. Encode the supplied coefficients for rxn_002, rxn_003, rxn_005, rxn_008, rxn_011 and rxn_016. The larger coefficients arising from S8 bookkeeping are not themselves evidence of implausibility. Literature alignment is strong for the protected-cysteinyl chemistry and for acknowledging unresolved steps. Nevertheless, P1–P9 all require unvalidated terminal transformations, particularly rxn_014 and rxn_015, together with rxn_012 or rxn_013; P7–P9 additionally require rxn_005. These shared gaps prevent the branches from establishing complete free-cysteine synthesis. P10 supplies experimental target-identification evidence, but not a quantified, independently replicated source with demonstrated environmental accumulation. Surface staging and protected handling are chemically sensible constraints, yet reaction-specific conditions, reagent availability, Mg2+ conditions, separation procedures and atmospheric deposition survival remain insufficiently specified. Add reaction-level citations and distinguish measured transformations from proposed extensions. Overall confidence reflects these network-level bottlenecks and the empirical haze evidence, not the number of pathways, shared molecules or environmental stages.
